A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ParaS2S research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original S2S benchmark results, human evaluations, RL ablations, annotation-budget experiments, and real-speech transfer results.

after.justification: v2 retains original model and human-evaluation results and adds experiments comparing automatic judges and ablating PolyTone and style information.

M1.justification: v2 introduces PolyTone training of acoustic analysts using identical linguistic content spoken in different styles, substantially extending the automatic judge beyond v1's annotated-input pipeline. Section 5.2 specifies predicted input styles for reward-model distillation. The underlying Kimi-Audio, SFT, reward-model distillation, and GRPO framework remains.

E1.justification: v1 Appendix F's explicit IEMOCAP-to-MELD and reverse training-transfer scenarios are no longer reported. Both real-speech test sets, the four synthetic paralinguistic categories, and VoiceBench remain. PolyTone uses the existing style categories without adding a new language or benchmark domain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds gpt-audio as an evaluated end-to-end automatic-judge baseline, a comparison absent from v1. The comparator rosters in the retained S2S and TTS response comparisons remain unchanged; the GPT-4o naming edits accompany identical result rows.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled judge comparisons varying known versus predicted input attributes, output emotion/tone information, and PolyTone versus unique-content training. It specifies O5 for reward-model distillation and ground-truth-input O2 for benchmarking. v1's constrained/unconstrained reward-data settings and fixed annotation-budget protocol disappear. These are changes to reported experimental design, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 2 ablations investigate which style information and training strategy improve agreement with humans. Section 5.2 also adds a qualitative observation of overfitting after extended SFT. The fixed-budget allocation study and real-speech adaptation/transfer analysis are removed. Existing GRPO hyperparameter sweeps and VoiceBench analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix E reports p-values for the judge–human correlations; v2's expanded correlation table omits significance testing. Neither version reports training-seed variation or confidence intervals for the main model comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds judge correlations, including averages of 0.618 for gpt-audio and 0.723 versus 0.701 for predicted-input judging with versus without PolyTone. Figure 2(a)'s RL curve changes, while budget-allocation and transfer results disappear. The retained automatic-scoring, expert-ranking, and crowd-evaluation tables have identical numerical entries. O2's 0.776 category average is not a demonstrated improvement over v1's differently summarized 0.773 'All' correlation.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, training objectives, GRPO advantage calculation, and KL expression are retained, largely relocated to v2 Appendix A.4. PolyTone adds a conceptual training rationale, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 makes PolyTone, reduced style hallucination, and superiority over end-to-end audio-LLM judging central contributions, presenting RL partly as validation of the judge. v1 primarily foregrounded the RL framework and annotation efficiency. v2 also claims over 10% improvement under both objective and subjective evaluation, although its retained human-evaluation appendix still reports 7.6%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of content-driven style hallucination, the distinction between emotional state and conversational tone, and why PolyTone helps emotion and sarcasm most. It adds an overfitting explanation for shortened responses after extended SFT. Interpretations concerning annotation-budget allocation and cross-corpus RL transfer are removed with their analyses.

D1.justification: v2 supplies acoustic-classifier identities and checkpoint links, PolyTone training-data quantities and hardware, a newly disclosed two-epoch SFT warmup, and majority-vote aggregation of expert ratings. Most existing SFT/RM/GRPO hyperparameters are relocated unchanged. The explicit IEMOCAP session split disappears with the transfer study.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against audio-LLM judges through Chiang et al. and SpeechJudge, adds OmniChat, and cites literature distinguishing emotion, tone, and speech acts. These additions support the evaluator emphasis, while the existing discussion of S2S models, RL, and dialogue benchmarks remains largely intact.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten around automatic-judge validation. Related-work subsections are reordered, detailed dataset construction and RL formulations move into appendices, and six experimental subsections become two broader sections. The appendices are reorganized from A–I into A.1–A.8.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, the judge-ablation table is added, and Figure 2 replaces the budget-allocation panel with the existing VoiceBench comparison, also retained in the appendix. Examples move into the main text, tables are restructured or removed, and appendix prompts become formatted boxes within the new conference layout. The GRPO ablation graphics themselves remain identical.

improvement.justification: New Table 2 strengthens validation of the central automatic judge through a competing evaluator and controlled style-information and PolyTone ablations, improving on v1's evaluation of its selected pipeline alone. The net gain is limited by lost significance and training-transfer reporting and by the new claim of over 10% subjective improvement despite the unchanged 7.6% appendix result.
